claims.text: Elevated-temperature wear resistance of high-entropy-alloy protective coatings is governed by formation of a protective surface oxide layer.
The wear-protective oxide layer is coherent and self-adherent.
The protective oxide is enriched in Al, Cr, or Ti.
The oxide acts as a hard, low-shear barrier against mechanical abrasion.
An as-deposited AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 coating is predisposed to rapid oxidation in oxygen at high temperature.
Oxidizing and inert atmospheres, or pre-oxidized and non-pre-oxidized samples, should be compared under otherwise identical wear conditions.
At approximately 400–600 °C, oxidation kinetics are sufficiently rapid to form the proposed oxide during reciprocating wear.
The surface mediator is a continuous, coherent oxide layer.
The protective layer may comprise Cr2O3, Al2O3, or TiO2.
The oxide develops preferentially along phase boundaries or at particular elemental sites.
In an oxygen-rich environment, selected alloy elements oxidize to form the protective film.
The oxide film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
Formation of the oxide film attenuates wear.
Formation of the oxide film lowers the coefficient of friction.
Without oxygen or sufficient oxide formation, the bare HEA surface is more susceptible to mechanical damage.
HEA coatings tested in air will have lower wear rates than otherwise identical coatings tested in argon.
HEA coatings tested in air will have lower coefficients of friction than otherwise identical coatings tested in argon.
Inert conditions produce minimal oxide formation.
The mechanism should apply to HEA coatings containing protective-oxide-forming elements over roughly 400–600 °C.
Failure to observe improved wear and friction in air, or failure to detect a coherent oxide in the air-tested samples, is specified as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial-state and mechanism fields describe rapid in-situ oxidation of an as-deposited coating in oxygen at high temperature, whereas the baseline groups 'without pre-oxidation' with inert conditions and says minimal oxide forms. A non-pre-oxidized sample tested in hot air could still oxidize rapidly, so absence of pre-oxidation is not equivalent to absence of oxygen.
